ety.text: From Middle English narow, narowe, narewe, narwe, naru, from Old English nearu (“narrow, strait, confined, constricted, not spacious, limited, petty; limited, poor, restricted; oppressive, causing anxiety (of that which restricts free action of body or mind), causing or accompanied by difficulty, hardship, oppressive; oppressed, not having free action; strict, severe”), from Proto-West Germanic *naru, from Proto-Germanic *narwaz (“constricted, narrow”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ner- (“to turn, bend, twist, constrict”).
From Middle English narwen (“to narrow”); see there for more details, but ultimately derived from the noun.

senses.d: Having a small width; not wide; having opposite edges or sides that are close, especially by comparison to length or depth.
ex: a narrow hallway

senses.d: Of little extent; very limited; circumscribed.
ex: The Jews were but a small nation, and confined to a narrow compass in the world.

senses.d: Restrictive; without flexibility or latitude.
ex: a narrow interpretation

senses.d: Having a small margin or degree.
ex: a narrow escape
The Republicans won by a narrow majority.

senses.d: Limited as to means; straitened
ex: narrow circumstances

senses.d: Parsimonious; niggardly; covetous; selfish.
ex: a very narrow […] and stinted charity

senses.d: Scrutinizing in detail; close; accurate; exact.
ex: But first with narrow search I must walk round / This garden, and no corner leave unspied.

senses.d: Formed (as a vowel) by a close position of some part of the tongue in relation to the palate; or (according to Bell) by a tense condition of the pharynx; distinguished from wide.
Of or supporting only those text characters that can fit into the traditional 8-bit representation.
ex: a narrow character; a narrow stream

senses.d: A narrow passage, especially a contracted part of a stream, lake, or sea; a strait connecting two bodies of water.
ex: the narrows of New York harbor
Near the island lay on one side the jaws of a dangerous narrow.

senses.d: To reduce in width or extent; to contract.
ex: We need to narrow the search.

senses.d: To get narrower.
ex: The road narrows.

senses.d: To partially lower one's eyelids in a way usually taken to suggest a defensive, aggressive or penetrating look.
ex: He stepped in front of me, narrowing his eyes to slits.
She wagged her finger in his face, and her eyes narrowed.

senses.d: To contract the size of, as a stocking, by taking two stitches into one.
To convert to a data type that cannot hold as many distinct values.
ex: to narrow an int variable to a short variable

grp.label: to reduce in width or extent

senses.d: Telling a story.
Overly talkative; garrulous.
ex: But wise through time, and narrative with age.

senses.d: Of or relating to narration.
ex: the narrative thrust of a film

senses.d: The systematic recitation of an event or series of events.
That which is narrated.
A representation of an event or story in a way to promote a certain point of view.
ex: changing, controlling the narrative
The posters quickly became embroiled in the interminable battle over narrative in the Israel-Palestine conflict.

senses.d: A manner of conveying a story, fictional or otherwise, in a body of work.
ex: The plot is full of holes, but the narrative is extremely compelling.
